# Fast and slow: System One models and Jev {#sec-ch07}

::: {.epigraph by="David Hume, 1748"}
A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence.
:::

TypeSafe didn't call Jev a better LLM. It called it the first of a new class: a *System One* model [@typesafe2026]. Is that a real idea, or a clever name? Both. This chapter explains the idea, then separates what we actually know about Jev from what's only claimed.

::: {.goals}
- Describe System 1 and System 2, in people and in software.
- Route cases by doubt between a fast and a slow system.
- Sort claims about a new model into three piles.
:::

## Two ways of thinking

What's 2 + 2? The answer was just there. Now 17 × 24. That felt different: you had to stop and work in steps. The psychologist Daniel Kahneman called these **System 1**, fast and automatic, and **System 2**, slow and effortful [@kahneman2011]. System 1 runs almost everything you do and is usually right, but it can be confidently wrong. (A bat and a ball cost \$1.10; the bat costs \$1.00 more than the ball. The ball isn't 10 cents [@frederick2005].)

Software maps onto this surprisingly well. Rules and classifiers are System 1: fast, good at familiar patterns. LLMs, especially "reasoning" ones, are the nearest thing to System 2: slow, general, and paid for by the token. For years the industry has used System 2 machinery for everything, including the thousands of quick judgements a day that System 1 handles well.

![Tasks in and around a SOC, placed by how often they happen and how much thinking each needs (illustrative). The frequent ones are grouped at the bottom right: quick judgements made hundreds or thousands of times a day. The few that need real reasoning happen rarely.](/figures/ch15/task-map.pdf){#fig-task-map}

::: {.keyidea}
Most of the work is System 1 work, but most of the machinery we use is System 2.
:::

## Route by doubt

With a fast system and a slow one, how do you split the work? A good expert sorts most cases in seconds and *notices* the ones that don't feel right. So: let the fast system see everything, and send only the cases it's unsure about to the slow one.

![Expected cost per day as more alerts go to System 2. Sending the alerts System 1 is least sure about (green, solid line) gets most of the benefit early. Sending a random share (grey, dashed line) gets almost nothing until you send nearly everything.](/figures/ch15/routing-curve.pdf){#fig-routing-curve}

On our alerts, sending the 20% that System 1 is least sure about gets {{< num ch15 share_gain_20 pct >}} of everything a perfect investigation could add. A random 20% gets {{< num ch15 share_gain_20_random pct >}} (@fig-routing-curve). And you pay the slow price only on that 20%.

::: {.keyidea}
A fast system is valuable in two ways: its speed, and knowing which cases it shouldn't decide.
:::

This only works if the fast system is *calibrated*: its 0.5 must really mean "could go either way". An overconfident System 1 keeps the dangerous cases for itself. Kahneman and the psychologist Gary Klein, after years on opposite sides, agreed on when fast judgement can be trusted: a regular world, lots of practice, and quick, clear feedback [@kahneman2009]. For machines I'd add a fourth condition: honest doubt.

![Conditions under which fast, intuitive judgement tends to be reliable, adapted from Kahneman and Klein. SOC triage mostly meets the first three. The fourth is what separates good experts, and good models, from confident ones.](/figures/ch15/conditions.pdf){#fig-conditions}

## What we know about Jev: three piles

I've never called Jev; it was in early access when I wrote this. What I had was its official Python library (anyone can read it), its documentation, the launch coverage and early papers. How much can anyone say from the outside? More than you'd think, less than most articles suggest. The trick is to sort every claim into three piles.

![Every claim about Jev in this book, sorted into three piles. The first pile you can check yourself today. The second is what TypeSafe says. The third is what nobody outside the company can know yet.](/figures/ch16/ledger.pdf){#fig-ledger}

::: {.keyidea}
Sort every claim about a new model into three piles: verified, vendor-reported and unknown.
:::

**Verified: the interface.** You send one request with three things: the **state** (the situation, as text or structured data), the **model** name, and a set of named, typed **questions**. You get back, for each question, a typed answer with a probability for every option. There are three question types: yes/no, pick-one and rate-on-a-scale (Chapter 8).

![A real request as the official SDK builds it, and the response. The answers here come from the book's stand-in, but their shape is just what the SDK's own data models expect.](/figures/ch16/anatomy.pdf){#fig-anatomy-09}

**Vendor-reported: two ideas.** A "parallel sampler" that produces all its outputs in one pass instead of word by word, which TypeSafe says is where the speed comes from. And a training method, **RLCD**, said to reward *calibrated* probabilities. We don't know the details. But Chapter 2 tells you how such a reward could work: a proper scoring rule makes honesty the best strategy. That's my reasoning, not something TypeSafe has published.

**Unknown:** model size, design and training data; calibration on *your* data; behaviour on attacker-written input; how behaviour changes between versions. Exactly what a decision layer depends on most.

## Check the numbers against each other

TypeSafe reports a response time of about 70 to 500 milliseconds and a price of \$0.042 per million input tokens, with output free. At 500 tokens a decision, that's about \$21 per million decisions, against roughly \$660 at this book's illustrative mid-range LLM price. Real LLM prices vary a hundredfold, so treat the ratio as a size, not a fact. And always ask of speed claims: *faster than what, doing what?* A non-reasoning LLM asked for a one-word label is far closer than a reasoning one [@regolo2026].

::: {.keyidea}
When a vendor gives you several numbers, check whether they agree with each other.
:::

In TypeSafe's launch demo, Jev played the video game *Doom*, about ten decisions a second at a reported \$7 an hour. That's 36,000 decisions an hour, about \$0.0002 each, which at the listed price means about 4,600 tokens of game description per decision: plausible. The numbers agree. That doesn't prove them; if they had implied three tokens, or three million, you'd have learned something.

::: {.keyidea}
Unknowns about a new model aren't reasons to avoid it; they're reasons to test it on your own data.
:::

::: {.breaks}
The two-systems idea is a metaphor, not a fact about the brain, and a System One model isn't "intuitive"; it's a trained function. Routing by doubt fails when the fast system is confidently wrong about a whole kind of case, such as a new attack it has never seen; random audits and drift checks are there to catch what doubt misses. And vendor numbers come from the vendor's tasks, setup and comparisons; early-access models change fast, so pin a version and recheck.
:::

:::
